newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian campaign quiet, one isolated clash.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian campaign quiet, one isolated clash.

text.p: Indonesia's violence-marred campaign for May 29 general elections resumed on a quieter note on Wednesday, with only one report of an isolated clash between students and supporters of the ruling Golkar party.
Witnesses said some 2,000 students of the IAIN Islamic University on the southern outskirts of Jakarta threw stones at Golkar supporters after an altercation just outside the campus.
The students retreated into the campus after detachments of marine commandos and riot police arrived on the scene and charged them with batons, the witnesses said.
There were no serious injuries or arrests.

Widespread violence has erupted across the country's main Java island over the past four days as the campaign heads into the home stretch, and authorities have blamed a left-wing group outside the country's rigid political system for the clashes.
The Australian, U.S. and British embassies advised their citizens in Jakarta to be on guard against further violence.

Lieutenant-General Syarwan Hamid, head of the military's socio-political section, was quoted by the official Antara news agency on Wednesday as blaming the illegal left-wing People's Democratic Party (PRD) for the campaign disturbances.
"I have come to the conclusion we must suspect the PRD as being behind the acts of violence," Hamid told a closed-door meeting of media editors on Tuesday.

"The phenomena and indications of the PRD's involvement in the riots are there," he said, refering to leaflets found at campaign rallies advocating replacing the government and current political laws, including those that give the military a powerful role in internal affairs.

Indonesia allows only Golkar, the Moslem-based United Development Party (PPP) and the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) to contest elections. They are required to swear to abide by state ideology and refrain from open criticism of the government and the political system.

Hamid had also blamed the PRD for riots that broke out in Jakarta in July last year after PDI chief Megawati Sukarnoputri, daughter of the late founding president Sukarno, was ousted by a government-backed faction.
Most PRD leaders were arrested and subsquently convicted of subversion. Twelve of its most senior leaders have been sentenced to up to 13 years in prison.

Most of the violence during the campaign has involved clashes between PPP and Golkar supporters. The PPP, whose ranks have been swelled by an informal alliance with Megawati supporters, has also clashed several times with security forces.

The Republika newspaper reported on Wednesday that Adam Khaeruddin, 20, was fatally shot while watching disturbances in the Warung Buncit area of south Jakarta the previous day. It did not say who shot him, but witnesses said both police and troops fired into the air to disperse a few thousand PPP supporters.
Neither hospitals nor police were immediately available for comment.
The government has not acknowledged any deaths in the violence, although the Kompas daily on Wednesday quoted Hamid as saying 110 people had died in accidents during the campaign.
Hamid said 83 people had died in traffic accidents and 27 drowned when their boat sank on the way to a Golkar rally.
